all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: computer
concepts.definition: A computer is one of the major components of virtual reality (VR) hardware, a device that processes data from input sensors and activates output devices so that a user can perceive the world.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a computer or processing device is used in a broad sense to mean a device that processes inputs and produces outputs for the user to perceive the world.
In a virtual reality (VR) system, the processing part or computer is a device that processes data from input sensors and, based on that processing, activates or actuates output devices.

The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.

The major components of a computer used as the processing element in a virtual reality (VR) system are the graphics processing unit (GPU), the central processing unit (CPU), and random access memory (RAM).

concepts.name: output device
concepts.definition: An output device is an XR hardware component that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs, not only a visual display; examples include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms, and treadmills.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).
In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a display or output device is used in a broad sense to mean any device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, not only a visual display.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.
A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.
The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

concepts.name: input device
concepts.definition: Input device is XR hardware that captures or tracks a user's input, actions, or positions and sends that data to an XR system for processing.

defining_facts.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

concepts.name: interaction
concepts.definition: Interaction is the activity that takes place between a user and a system, often by manipulating an image or parts of it with input devices. In immersive environments it is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and system control.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
Interaction in non-immersive settings, such as augmented reality (AR), is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture.

For immersive virtual reality (VR) or mixed reality (MR) experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence.

Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: software development kit
concepts.definition: Software development kit (SDK) is a platform-dependent installable package of software development tools for a specific hardware and operating system combination that provides fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual or augmented reality experiences.

defining_facts.text: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

To build a virtual reality (VR) experience, a developer can either build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch using a basic software development kit (SDK) for a specific headset, device, or platform, or use a ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) customized by choosing menu options and writing high-level scripts.

A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required.

Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch gives the developer maximum control and the ability to optimize performance because the developer can choose and implement the algorithms for physics support according to performance, rather than being forced to use whatever comes with a package.

Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch imposes a difficult implementation burden and requires a lot of effort to understand and implement the overall system from scratch.

Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms.

Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.

Different head-mounted displays (HMDs) use different virtual reality (VR) software development kits (SDKs): the HTC Vive system can use the OpenVR SDK by Valve, the SteamVR SDK, or the VRTK SDK; the Oculus Rift uses the Oculus SDK; the Samsung Gear VR uses the Oculus Mobile SDK; the Sony PlayStation uses the PSVR SDK; and Google Daydream View or Google Cardboard uses the Google VR SDK.
The Google virtual reality (VR) software development kit (SDK) is open source but is no longer very much supported.

If a system is to be deployed on a specified hardware platform, head-mounted display (HMD), or smart glasses, and that platform provides features or functions not included in the built-in support provided by the Unity environment, the developer imports software development kits (SDKs) or packages to access and use those platform-specific functions.

In the Unity layered architecture, the application is the top layer, and the software development kit (SDK) layer, which is positioned on top of the Unity layer, is treated as part of the installed Unity package whose application programming interfaces (APIs) are used.

Vuforia is an augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) primarily meant to help developers deal with object recognition or computer vision issues, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking.

The basic steps for integrating a software development kit (SDK) into the Unity development environment are to install Unity Hub, import the SDK package into the Unity environment, use the functions of both Unity and the SDK, and then compile, build, and deploy.

concepts.name: graphics processing unit
concepts.definition: Graphics processing unit (GPU) is a parallel hardware component of a graphics card, with its own memory, that speeds up the rendering process by exploiting the inherent parallelism of graphics operations.

defining_facts.text: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).
A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the hardware component that is used for speeding up the rendering process.

In a typical virtual reality (VR) system that uses a game engine as middleware, the layers from lowest to highest are hardware, rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), game engine, and application software, and the hardware layer includes a graphics processing unit (GPU), a central processing unit (CPU), and memory.

An audio engine can perform its calculations on a central processing unit (CPU) or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), so it does not require a graphics processing unit (GPU), and audio engines are not typically associated with a GPU because a GPU is generally associated with graphics or rendering.

A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the processing unit of a separate graphics card, with its own memory elements, that is used in computer graphics and virtual reality to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations, which are highly parallel, whereas central processing units (CPUs) are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities, although modern CPUs have some parallel features.

A GPU is typically a multicore system in which many cores, each capable only of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic, work simultaneously on one single instruction and produce data simultaneously, and groups of cores form streaming multiprocessor units, each containing several cores.

A GPU is broadly organized with a host, input assemblers and a thread execution manager, where the manager allocates work to many streaming multiprocessors, each of which has a parallel data cache, and a texture storage stores predefined surface colors, with the elements exchanging data with global memory through load and store information.

The GPU performs modeling transformation by applying transformations such as rotation, multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, producing a stream of transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates, which gives a significant performance gain in real-time rendering because millions of vertices need to be processed per second and even more for a realistic immersive experience.

Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input.
Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles.
The GPU computes vertex color by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.

The GPU projection stage combines viewing transformation, projection transformation and viewport transformation in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices, producing a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates, a continuous coordinate space, ready to be converted to pixels.

In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.
In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities that take place are surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

In the pixel processing stage, the simplest surface texturing method applies stored texture images to the geometry being rendered by replacing the computed pixel color with the texture color at the corresponding texture point; GPUs store textures in high-speed texture storage on the graphics card, which each pixel calculation must access, and because nearby pixels tend to access nearby texture image locations, specialized memory caches reduce access time.

concepts.name: rendering
concepts.definition: Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.

defining_facts.text: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.
In the context of creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the terms view or rendering are used in a broad sense to refer not only to visual output but also to output for other senses.

From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.
The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

Image generation is a multi-stage computational process, and if all rendering-related computations were carried out by the central processing unit (CPU), the CPU's time would be consumed by rendering, leaving it with very little time for other tasks and the system could do little except rendering; to avoid this and increase efficiency, rendering is usually carried out by a dedicated component.

The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

Rendering, the key component of any immersive experience in which the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device, is covered by computer graphics, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.

concepts.name: computer graphics
concepts.definition: Computer graphics (CG) is the area that addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models. It creates or represents objects, synthesizes them into a scene, allows users to manipulate images on a screen, creates the perception of motion, and renders the scene on a display so humans can perceive it.

defining_facts.text: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.

One possibility for creating a virtual world is texture mapping, in which camera images of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object; this is a common computer-graphics operation that virtual reality (VR) software should ideally support.

For a good virtual reality (VR) immersive experience, client-end hardware is needed to support requirements arising from rendering or computer graphics and to manage rendering or computer graphics related issues, and the complexity required to render a scene corresponds to the need for high-end hardware support.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.
The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to create or represent objects, synthesize objects into a scene, and render the scene on a computer display so that humans can perceive it.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: interactive system
concepts.definition: Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.
Designers of interactive systems that are intended to be used by laypersons should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.

concepts.name: resource optimization
concepts.definition: Resource optimization is the technological optimization of resource requirements in extended reality (XR), including virtual reality (VR), that minimizes those requirements while maximizing immersive experience without compromising it. It generally focuses on client-end hardware so users can have a good experience with affordable hardware.

defining_facts.text: Optimization in virtual reality (VR) can be considered from two perspectives: optimized experience, that is, psychophysiological experience optimization, and optimized resource utilization or resource requirement, that is, technological optimization; these requirements are present in any extended reality (XR) system, but they gain more prominence in an immersive experience.

In virtual reality (VR), effective resource optimization means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience, without compromising it and, to the extent possible, without reducing its quality; this requires balancing the trade-offs between resource requirements and experience.
The objectives of virtual reality (VR) resource optimization are to minimize resource requirements without compromising the VR experience, that is, to maximize the VR experience.

Virtual reality (VR) resource optimization generally does not try to optimize every resource, assumes some resources are given, and instead focuses on hardware requirements at the client end (the user end), because focusing on client-end hardware is the most straightforward way to optimize resources without being entangled in many issues; the objective is for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.

never_defined.name: hardware
never_defined.definition: Hardware is a part of an extended reality (XR) system, including input devices, output devices, processing devices, central processing units, graphics processing units, and memory.

never_defined.name: software
never_defined.definition: Software is a resource in extended reality that is used to process input data, generate output data, and create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment.

never_defined.name: screen
never_defined.definition: A screen is a display on which an image or content is shown so that a human can perceive it.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional image
never_defined.definition: A Two-dimensional image is a representation of a scene that can be presented by a display device and that stereoscopic vision can make a user perceive as a three-dimensional object or space.

never_defined.name: smartphone
never_defined.definition: A smartphone is a familiar handheld device used for augmented reality; when placed in a cardboard virtual reality headset, it displays stereoscopic views, and it can also serve as the processing element of a virtual reality system.

never_defined.name: joystick
never_defined.definition: A joystick is a non-motion, world-grounded hand input device that is fixed in the real world, is commonly used to interact with grounded systems, and is used to navigate or teleport.

never_defined.name: central processing unit
never_defined.definition: Central processing unit (CPU) is a major component of a computer used as the processing element in a VR system that handles many tasks and passes graphics rendering tasks to a GPU.

never_defined.name: virtual reality experience
never_defined.definition: Virtual reality experience is an experience that utilizes human senses, created by virtual reality software driving hardware to generate appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs.

never_defined.name: animation
never_defined.definition: Animation is computer graphics content or an asset used for creating the perception of motion and in representing objects or complex characters.

never_defined.name: interface
never_defined.definition: An interface is the way a system interfaces with users, its environment, and other systems, letting users provide input, see outcomes, and act on outcomes; on a computer screen it is the whole content seen there.

never_defined.name: hertz
never_defined.definition: Hertz (Hz) is the unit used to measure frequency and represent refresh rate.

never_defined.name: object
never_defined.definition: An object is a part of a computer graphics image or scene that may be a three-dimensional model or interface object and is created, represented, synthesized, and rendered.

never_defined.name: switch
never_defined.definition: A switch is a physical controller used in interactive methods for system control.

never_defined.name: icon
never_defined.definition: An icon is an interface object that can be used to indicate user categories or provide information.

never_defined.name: resource requirement
never_defined.definition: Resource requirement is the technological optimization concern of an XR system, which is generally resource-hungry and whose resource requirements are minimized without compromising the immersive experience.

never_defined.name: manpower
never_defined.definition: Manpower is one of the resources in extended reality, especially virtual reality, and can include staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing.

never_defined.name: supporting infrastructure
never_defined.definition: Supporting infrastructure is a resource in extended reality, particularly virtual reality, and in virtual reality it includes rooms to store hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure.

never_defined.name: development tool
never_defined.definition: A Development tool is one kind of software resource in extended reality and virtual reality.

never_defined.name: software package
never_defined.definition: A software package is a type of software resource that can be included in extended reality, and particularly virtual reality.

never_defined.name: application package
never_defined.definition: An application package is a software resource in extended reality, particularly virtual reality.

never_defined.name: network infrastructure
never_defined.definition: Network infrastructure is a type of supporting infrastructure in virtual reality, with examples such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

never_defined.name: network gear
never_defined.definition: Network gear is an example of the network infrastructure included in the supporting infrastructure for virtual reality (VR) systems.

never_defined.name: router
never_defined.definition: A router is part of the network infrastructure included among supporting infrastructure in virtual reality.

never_defined.name: wire
never_defined.definition: A Wire is an example of network infrastructure included in the supporting infrastructure for VR.

never_defined.name: server
never_defined.definition: A server is part of the network infrastructure included in the supporting infrastructure for extended reality (XR) and virtual reality (VR).

never_defined.name: resource type
never_defined.definition: Resource type is a kind of resource in extended reality (XR) that can be optimized separately.

never_defined.name: hardware requirement
never_defined.definition: Hardware requirement is the client-end hardware resource that virtual reality resource optimization generally focuses on so that end users can have a good experience with affordable hardware.

never_defined.name: client-end hardware
never_defined.definition: Client-end hardware is hardware needed to support rendering and computer graphics requirements and to manage related issues for a good virtual reality immersive experience.

never_defined.name: interface object
never_defined.definition: An Interface object is one of the geometric objects, such as menus and icons, in the image of the whole interface displayed on a computer screen.

never_defined.name: menu
never_defined.definition: A menu is an interface object that is part of the image displayed on a computer screen.

never_defined.name: representation
never_defined.definition: Representation is used in computer graphics to represent objects or parts of an image, either as zeros and ones understood by computers or as realistic imagery perceived by humans.

never_defined.name: synthesis
never_defined.definition: Synthesis is one of the basic issues of computer graphics, in which objects are synthesized into a scene or parts of an image are synthesized to form complete realistic imagery.

never_defined.name: host computer
never_defined.definition: A host computer is a part of a generic graphics system that communicates with the display controller by sending display commands and possibly receiving interaction data.

never_defined.name: display command
never_defined.definition: Display command is a command sent by the CPU of a generic graphics system to a display controller.

never_defined.name: interaction data
never_defined.definition: Interaction data is data that a host computer may receive from a display controller in a generic graphics system.

never_defined.name: analog voltage
never_defined.definition: Analog voltage is a voltage required to activate pixels on a screen when a video controller converts a digital image.

never_defined.name: graphic device
never_defined.definition: A graphic device is a device that is broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan and raster scan devices.

never_defined.name: geometric primitive
never_defined.definition: A geometric primitive is a continuous part, such as a line or curve, that vector scan devices view an image as composed of.

never_defined.name: line
never_defined.definition: A line is a continuous geometric primitive, a geometric shape, that is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

never_defined.name: curve
never_defined.definition: A curve is a continuous geometric primitive that can be represented by a higher-degree polynomial or by smoothly joined lower-degree polynomial pieces in spline representation.

never_defined.name: precision
never_defined.definition: Precision is the level required by vector scan devices to target and excite specific pixels, and raster scan rendering requires less precision.

never_defined.name: vector scan rendering
never_defined.definition: Vector scan rendering is a type of scan rendering that requires more precision and is much more expensive than raster scan rendering.

never_defined.name: television
never_defined.definition: Television is a commercial product that typically comprises a raster scan display.

never_defined.name: memory location
never_defined.definition: A memory location is a part of a frame buffer that stores the intensity value for one pixel as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

never_defined.name: bit string
never_defined.definition: A bit string is a string of 0s and 1s used by a frame buffer in a raster scan system to store a pixel's intensity.

never_defined.name: virtual reality screen
never_defined.definition: Virtual reality screen is a screen in a virtual reality experience that is much closer to the eyes than a screen in typical computer usage.

never_defined.name: red
never_defined.definition: Red is one of the three primary colors whose light intensity, with green and blue, combines to produce the observed color in color displays and colored light-source models.

never_defined.name: green
never_defined.definition: Green is one of the red, green, and blue components of light intensity in a colored light source model and one of the primary colors emitted by a color display.

never_defined.name: blue
never_defined.definition: Blue is one of the red, green, and blue primary color components in a color display or colored light source model, whose intensity combines with the red and green components to form a perceived color.
